newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel braces for more Palestinian violence.
newsitem.headline: Israel braces for more Palestinian violence.

text.p: Israel said it feared more violent Palestinian protests against its construction of a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem would erupt on Friday.
"We have information the Palestinians will try during or after Moslem Friday prayers in the mosques to instigate violence," Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai told reporters.
"We do not want this to happen but we are ready for any possibility in all areas where we are in charge."

Palestinians enraged by the start of work on a 6,500-unit Jewish housing project at Jabal Abu Ghneim, or Har Homa, in East Jerusalem threw petrol bombs and rocks at soldiers near Bethlehem in the West Bank on Thursday.

The Israeli troops responded with rubber bullets and teargas in clashes reminscent of a six-year Palestinian uprising ended by a 1993 interim peace deal which the PLO charges the right-wing Israeli government has now violated.

Israel captured East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war and views all the city as its capital. The Palestine Liberation Organisation sees East Jerusalem as capital of a future Palestinian state and says Israel is trying to predetermine its final status.

On the diplomatic front, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu purused his proposal to skip further interim peace moves and finish "final status" talks on a permanent accord with the PLO within six months, nearly two years earlier than planned.

The Palestinians, who hope three Israeli interim pullbacks due to be completed by mid-1998 will leave them in charge of nearly all of the West Bank and Gaza, have rejected the offer as a trick to deflect world attention from the Jerusalem situation.

Netanyahu sent top aide Dore Gold to Egypt for talks with Osama el-Baz, President Hosni Mubarak's foreign policy adviser, Osama el-Baz. Palestinian President Yasser Arafat also was in Cairo for talks with Mubarak.
"I'm here to convey a message from Israel to Egypt and we have a very new proposal about the peace process to discuss," Gold told reporters.

"His (Gold's) proposals are unconvincing," Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa told Reuters. "I am unable now to say what these proposals are but I would like to tell you all that any ideas they are talking about that try to justify or circumvent what's happening in Jerusalem is rejected."
Netanyahu's communications director David Bar-Illan, defending the proposal to speed up "final status" talks, said Israel's interim agreements with the PLO had failed to narrow differences.
"So (Netanyahu) has suggested that we set ourselves a time limit of let's say six months and try to tackle the big issues and resolve them if possible in that period of time," he told Reuters.

"If that doesn't work, perhaps a situation in which there is some kind of mediation by the United States would come into consideration and there's always an option of returning to the arrangements of the interim period."
Under the interim peace deals, highly-sensitive issues such as the future of Jerusalem and Jewish settlements were left to be discussed only in "final status" talks.

White House press secretary Mark McCurry, who is with President Bill Clinton for a summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin in Helsinki, said Netanyahu's offer to finish making peace in six months could have value.

"We have always said that moving to the final status negotiations and beginning to deal with what are the most troublesome aspects of negotiations that the two sides have would be useful because that is where the greatest difficulty lies in resolving the differences that exist," he said.
At the United Nations, the Security Council held inconclusive consultations on a request by a 22-member Arab group for a meeting to demand that Israel halt the East Jerusalem housing project.
